source.title: DECEPTICON: How Dark Patterns Manipulate Web Agents
source.authors: Phil Cuvin; Hao Zhu; Di-Yi Yang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies model size and inference-time reasoning budgets and reports web-task success rates, a different measure from pretraining loss that bears on downstream task performance (V6). It does not test the claimed loss laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling laws as motivation, then measures dark-pattern susceptibility and web-task success as model size or reasoning effort changes. It reports no held-out cross-entropy losses, power-law fits, small-run extrapolations, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Dark-pattern effectiveness results are recorded as findings about scaling-related susceptibility, not as evidence about the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Weak, incidental test of V6. The Qwen2.5-VL size sweep (3B–72B, which the paper says share pretraining data) reports task success on a new adversarial web-agent benchmark (Table 7). No loss, power-law fit or extrapolation is reported. The Gemini and o3 sweeps vary inference-time reasoning, not model scale or pretraining loss, so they do not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with additions. The authors conclude that scaling model size or test-time reasoning does not protect web agents from dark patterns. Dark-pattern effectiveness rises with Qwen size and Gemini thinking budget, and o3 shows no decrease (nor clear increase) with reasoning effort. Existing defenses (in-context prompting, guardrail models) only partially help.
record.recipe_differences: Measures web-task success and dark-pattern effectiveness across model sizes or inference-time reasoning settings, rather than held-out language-model loss or compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary across parameter sizes, reasoning-token budgets, and reasoning-effort levels. A separate modality ablation also reports different dark-pattern effectiveness by input modality.

fits_no_version.finding: Dark-pattern effectiveness rises with Qwen2.5-VL size (43.8%→73.7%) and with Gemini-2.5-Flash thinking budget (38.5%→71.2%). For o3 it stays roughly flat (67.2–70.2%) across reasoning effort.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In web agents, larger models or more reasoning can increase susceptibility to dark-pattern manipulation (inverse scaling of robustness), though not uniformly across models.

fits_no_version.finding: Task success under dark patterns is non-monotonic in test-time reasoning. Gemini-2.5-Flash SR is 16.4%/38.5%/26.9% at 256/2048/16384 tokens. o3 SR is about 40% at every effort level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream agent success does not improve monotonically with test-time reasoning budget in adversarial web tasks.

record.problems: The scaling sweeps report no uncertainty values in Tables 7–9. The parameter-size sweep uses four model sizes from one family, and the reasoning-budget and reasoning-effort sweeps each use one model. The measured outcome is web-task success or dark-pattern effectiveness, not language-model loss.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out from the directly reported size and reasoning scaling sweeps. The paper's other evaluations, including dark-pattern categories, defenses, and modality ablations, do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in other regimes.
No relation to pretraining loss. With only four size points and no fitted trend, whether gains are 'predictable' in form is not tested.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The Section 5 prose gives Qwen DP as 38.5%→73.7% and Gemini DP as 37.6%→71.2%, but Tables 7–8 give 43.8% and 38.5% for the low ends; the rows follow the tables. Tables 7–9 give no standard errors, although the paper says SE is reported throughout. Scaling laws are cited only as motivation. This is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss measurements across parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fits or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation experiment or loss-minimising parameter/token split.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No power-law tests for other modalities or training regimes.

Measures web-task success on the generated dark-pattern benchmark for selected model-size and inference-reasoning settings; it does not relate downstream performance to pretraining loss or establish a general scaling law.
No comparison of loss-law exponents, fitting choices, parameter-counting conventions, or loss-curve bending.

relation.reason: The study reports its own downstream success measurements across Qwen model sizes; these bear on V6, although no quantitative prediction or scaling-law fit is tested.

tranche.reason: The Qwen model-size sweep reports downstream task success in a new adversarial web-agent setting, providing incidental evidence on V6.

source_check.notes: Section 5 conflicts with Figure 2 and Tables 7–8 on starting DP values: prose gives Qwen 38.5% and Gemini 37.6%; the figure and tables give 43.8% and 38.5%. SR permits additional unwanted outcomes, so task completion is distinct from robustness; no power-law fit, extrapolation, or pretraining-loss test is reported.
